chapter_theme: Paripadal 9, to Sevvel at Parankunram: his birth from Siva and his wedding to Indra's daughter on the hill, a lesson to Vedic scholars in the Tamil order of love and the sulk, the quarrel of his two wives and their women's mock battle, contests of the performers, and closing praise of the lord of both karpu and love.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his birth and his hill: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:9:1-11.reading: The poet hails Murugan as born of the blue-throated lord who, when the high gods of the northern mountain agreed, took on his spread matted hair the great flood that the lord of the lotus let fall and held it lightly like a flower, and says that on the day the god married the doe-eyed daughter of the thousand-eyed Indra her flower eyes rained like drops of gems, and his own Parankunram took in the dark rain in the heart of summer and the cool rain did not stop.
paripadal:9:1-11.nuance: The wedding is marked by rain out of season: the bride's eyes raining and the hill's summer rain are set side by side, so the hill is made a sacred place by an event, not by nature. Indra's thousand eyes are counted as five times two hundred (ஐ-இருநூற்று), and line 8 answers with இரு நூற்று in the bride's own epithet. Siva's holding of the Ganga is told without naming the river.

comparisons.tenor: the flood held on Siva's hair
the tears of the bride's eyes

thinai_evidence.note: the passage defends the wife's sulk against the courtesan, the uri of marutham

paripadal:9:12-26.reading: The poet turns to the poets of truthful speech who expound the four Vedas and tells them the order of love: what excels is desire born of love, and within desire the bodily union of two who long alike; above the quarrel stands karpu, which holds within it the courtesan with her begging and giving, the courteous reproach, and the சுணங்கறை where the wife adorns herself and rejoices to make the courtesan who newly enjoyed his shoulders flush, words spoken in the house to trouble the husband, and the fruit of that too lies in the sulk; so women who never part are not at fault when they quarrel and sulk, and those who have not studied cool Tamil with its unshakable rule of porul will not take what this hill yields.
paripadal:9:12-26.nuance: The poet addresses Vedic scholars as outsiders and tells them that what this hill teaches is the porul grammar of Tamil, so the god's household quarrel that follows (lines 27 to 69) is offered as a lesson in akam theory, not as scandal. The ranking is a small treatise: love, then equal union, then karpu, with the courtesan and the sulk placed inside karpu rather than against it. சுணங்கறை is a rare word whose sense we cannot fix, and the clause order of lines 16 to 22 is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulk at the god who comes from another woman, marutham's uri on a kurinji hill

paripadal:9:27-44.reading: As the god comes in, his chest garland wreathed in the smoke of sandal that the river carried down breaking its banks, a bright pearl chain shining on him, one wife does not bow but says, 'Long live, Maaya, the fault is not yours: would you, who rest on the soft shoulders of the fortunate, deign to enjoy the beauty of plain women like us? The rain-grove will be trampled by what the sharp-toothed girls do'; then, pointing with her hand, crying 'don't come near', she binds tight and beats with her garland for a rod the woman who outdid her in the women's quarrel, the Vel who pays tribute with his head-garland touching her fine feet, and the woman who gives him her chest saying 'don't grieve'; and one wife's peacock closes with the other's bright peacock, the two parrots babble at the meeting, and a bee of the possessed god's hill leaps onto a thick hair-knot.
paripadal:9:27-44.nuance: 'The fault is not yours' is blame in the form of a blessing. The god who bows his garland to a woman's feet pays திறை, a conquered king's tribute, so the war god is defeated in love; in the closing line he is வெறி கொண்டான், the god of the possession rite, now the cause of a domestic fray. Who bows to whose feet is a reading: the three accusatives of lines 36 to 38 can be taken as the rival, the god and the rival again, and lines 33 and 34 are obscure.

comparisons.tenor: the garland she beats them with
the god bowing to a woman's feet

thinai_evidence.note: the poem itself calls the co-wives' play-fight a thumbai battle

paripadal:9:45-69.reading: The women of the two sides join in: they tangle garland with garland, swing their chaplets and stumble, lash with the bands of their breasts as whips, hurl balls wound with garlands, and, their innocent glances changed, their thin waists swaying, take the head of the fray, shifting into the gait of a musth elephant, coming on like horses in their course, as if sorting chariot ropes, bending striped bows to the chest, setting arrow against arrow and whirling bangles like discs, as the soft peacock-gaited women and the soft-spoken flower-eyed companions of the sky-king's daughter close round the broad-chested god; some bathe in the guarded pool, some pluck strings like honey-drinking bees, some spread their tails and dance like crested peacocks, some call like cuckoos, some raise a clamour; and because Valli's kin, the fierce hill-men of the kurinji, made of it a skilful thumbai battle, cool Parankunram became fit for the god of the victorious spear.
paripadal:9:45-69.nuance: The poem names the play-fight thumbai, the puram thinai of pitched battle, and gives it the full order of an army (elephant, horse, chariot, bow, arrow, disc) played with garlands, breastbands and balls: the war god's household quarrel is staged in war's own grammar, and the hill is said to befit him for that very reason. Lines 61 to 66 move from the fray to bathing, music and dance, perhaps the same women after the quarrel. Valli's hill kin take her side, so the co-wives' quarrel is also a quarrel of the hill against the sky.

comparisons.tenor: the women's gait in the fray

thinai_evidence.note: closing praise and prayer: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:9:70-85.reading: Addressing the warrior whose spear cut down fierce Sur at the root of his great mango form, the poet says that on the god's hill dancers outdo dancers, panar outdo those practised in song, the skilled the skilled and the unskilled the unskilled, and, as if at one word, a banner stands beside the cool pool that has taken in the fresh red flood, with spears and with victory flags raised high that hold the worth of valour; hailing the wondrous Kumara of a lineage worth loving, lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu, he says: we have praised you and with bowed heads worship you; may our service at your feet, which excels in our love for you, excel in its fruit and flourish day by day.
paripadal:9:70-85.nuance: Line 81 sets the god's two unions in one phrase, the bond of karpu and the bond of love, which closes the argument of lines 12 to 26: the god who holds both is the model of the order the poet taught the Vedic scholars. The contest of like with like (lines 72 to 75) mirrors the co-wives' quarrel: on this hill rivalry itself keeps its proper pairs. Line 79 is a repaired reading and its sense is thin.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 6 names the god only as husband of a bright-browed woman of spotless chastity (மறுவில் கற்பின் வாணுதற் கணவன்); Paripadal 9.8-11 names her as the daughter of the thousand-eyed one and sets the wedding at Parankunram, marked by rain in summer.
links.teaches: Held together, the guide poem's opening epithet turns out to rest on a wedding story that the Paripadal ties to one hill, which explains why Parankunram, the hill of that marriage, is the first abode the guide poem then visits.

links.note: Kural 1330 says sulking is love's pleasure and its pleasure is the embrace that follows; Paripadal 9.12-22 ranks love, equal union and karpu, and places the courtesan, the reproach and the சுணங்கறை inside karpu, with their fruit in the sulk (ஊடல்).
links.teaches: The Kural gives the sulk's worth as a man's two-line saying, while the Paripadal builds it into a ranked theory addressed to Vedic scholars and then uses it to excuse a god's wives, so the pair shows oodal already held as doctrine of Tamil porul, citable to outsiders and to the gods.

links.note: In both a wife refuses the husband who has been with other women: Kural 1311 says 'I will not come near your chest, philanderer' (நண்ணேன் பரத்தநின் மார்பு); in Paripadal 9.30-40 the wife blesses him ironically and cries 'don't come near' (குறுகல்), while the rival gives him her chest (மார்பு அளிப்பாளை).
links.teaches: The Kural's refusal is private and the rival only imagined, while the Paripadal stages the same refusal with the rival present and offering the very chest the wife denies, so the pair shows the one gesture of refusing the chest working as a quarrel between two women, not only between wife and husband.

links.note: Thiruppugazh 12, a Parankunram song, has Indra's daughter and the hunter girl both embrace Murugan's twelve shoulders; Paripadal 9 sets the same two wives at the same hill in a quarrel with blows of garlands.
links.teaches: The later hymn keeps the two consorts side by side in a single embrace, while the Sangam song lets them fight over him at the same shrine, which shows the co-wives' rivalry was once part of the hill's sacred lore and was smoothed away as the pair became fixed icons of devotion.

links.note: Thiruppugazh 18 names Murugan of south Parankunram as the one who took the girl the hill people gave (குன்றவர்கள் தந்தபெண்); Paripadal 9.67-69 has Valli's kin, the kurinji hill-men (குறிஞ்சிக் குன்றவர் ... வள்ளி தமர்), turn the wives' quarrel into a thumbai battle on that hill.
links.teaches: In the hymn the hill people appear only as givers of the bride, while in the Paripadal they stay her partisans after the marriage and fight for her against the sky-born wife, so the pair shows Valli's marriage remembered as an alliance with her kin that carried on into the god's household.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai 101-102 gives one of the six faces to smiling with Valli, the hill-dwellers' daughter, after its opening epithet for the chaste wife; Paripadal 9.81 names the god as lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu (கற்பு இணை நெறியூடு அற்பு இணைக் கிழமை).
links.teaches: The guide poem lists the two marriages separately, one as an epithet and one as a face's work, while the Paripadal joins them in one phrase after teaching the order of love, so the pair shows the two consorts being read as the two branches of akam, karpu and the love of free choice, united in one god.

source_issues: Paripadal 9: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.
Paripadal 9 lines 15 and 29 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 9 line 79: repaired from sangamtamil.com's reading (encoding junk or a lost first letter); the sense of மேஎ எஃகினவை is thin.
Paripadal 9 lines 3, 49 and 58: words run together without a space (சிமைஉயர்ந்தவர், நுசுப்பார்நூழில், அகலத்தவனைவானவன்).
Paripadal 9 lines 18-22: சுணங்கறை is a rare word and the passage may be corrupt; read with caution.
